articles.title: Lula Wins Brazil’s Runoff: Will Trump Escalate Tariffs and Sanctions? - Diplomacy and Law
articles.summary: Lula Wins Brazil’s Runoff: Will Trump Escalate Tariffs and Sanctions?  Diplomacy and Law
articles.full_text:
Lula's victory in Brazil's October 25, 2026, presidential runoff has renewed attention to the Lula–Trump tariffs dispute and the possibility of further American sanctions. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term after a campaign marked by disagreements over Brazil's relations with Washington. The election comes after Donald Trump's administration imposed substantial tariffs on Brazilian exports and previously sanctioned Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. The immediate question is whether Washington will increase economic pressure following Lula's reelection.
Trump retains legal instruments to impose additional tariffs, expand existing trade restrictions, or introduce new targeted sanctions. Lula's electoral victory, however, does not independently satisfy the statutory conditions for using those instruments. Any further measures would require decisions under applicable American legislation, while their international legality would depend on the specific obligations governing trade, economic coercion, and relations between sovereign states.
The dispute already extends beyond political disagreement. Brazil has initiated two proceedings against American tariffs at the World Trade Organization (WTO), including a July 2026 complaint challenging the Section 301 duties. Meanwhile, a February 2026 ruling of the U.S. Supreme Court restricted presidential authority to impose tariffs under emergency economic legislation. Bilateral negotiations have nevertheless continued, creating an alternative to further restrictions. Lula's reelection leaves Washington and Brasília facing an established trade confrontation, unresolved legal proceedings, and competing incentives for economic cooperation.
1. Lula’s Reelection and Washington’s Immediate Response
Lula's reelection preserves the Brazilian executive's existing foreign-policy leadership during a difficult period in U.S.–Brazil relations. The relationship deteriorated following American tariff measures and disagreements concerning decisions by Brazilian judicial authorities. Questions involving trade regulation, political expression, and the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro became entangled with economic policy, producing disputes that were already underway before the presidential campaign ended.
The election also carried diplomatic significance because Flávio Bolsonaro belonged to a political family with established connections to Trump and his political movement. A change of government in Brasília could have altered the political environment surrounding those disputes, although the applicable legal obligations would not have disappeared automatically. Lula's victory leaves negotiations in the hands of an administration that has consistently rejected the justification for the American Section 301 tariffs.
Washington's response must be distinguished from the political significance of the result. Criticism of Lula, expressions of sympathy for the Bolsonaro family, and formal decisions affecting Brazilian commerce have different consequences. The relevant evidence of escalation would be a new governmental measure, rather than an inference drawn from political relationships.
1.1 The Runoff Result and Lula’s Fourth Presidential Term
Brazil held its presidential runoff on October 25, 2026, after neither leading candidate obtained an absolute majority of valid votes in the first round. On October 4, Flávio Bolsonaro received 56,104,503 votes, or 47.03%, while Lula obtained 53,879,538 votes, or 45.16%, according to the completed first-round results published by the Superior Electoral Court, known as the Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). Bolsonaro entered the runoff ahead by approximately 2.22 million votes.
Lula reversed that result on October 25. The TSE's near-complete election-night returns placed him at approximately 51.8% of valid votes against 48.2% for Bolsonaro, with a lead approaching 4.4 million votes. The Associated Press subsequently reported the result after counting had been completed, confirming Lula's reelection. The figures establish the reversal of the first-round outcome without treating an earlier election-night snapshot as the exact final total.
The determination of the electoral winner is distinct from formal certification, known in Brazilian electoral law as diplomação. That procedure follows the rules established by the TSE and confirms the elected candidates' entitlement to assume office, subject to the applicable legal requirements. Constitutional Amendment No. 111/2021 changed the presidential inauguration date to January 5, beginning with the mandate resulting from the 2026 election. Lula's fourth term is consequently scheduled to begin on January 5, 2027.
The runoff was accompanied by controversy after Supreme Federal Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered an extension of voting amid difficulties involving transportation and severe weather. The TSE clarified on October 25 that voting would continue only where polling had not already closed at 5 p.m. The tribunal also stated that the receipt of polling-station records, totalization, and publication of results would resume after 7 p.m.
Any legal challenge arising from that decision falls within the jurisdiction of Brazil's competent electoral and judicial institutions. A controversy over voting procedures does not itself establish fraud or invalidate a presidential election. Under Article 77 of the Brazilian Constitution, the national electoral outcome is determined through Brazil's constitutional and electoral processes, not through recognition or approval by a foreign government.
1.2 Trump, the Bolsonaro Family, and the Election Result
Trump's relationship with the Bolsonaro family has influenced the political environment surrounding bilateral disputes. During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, the two leaders developed close public ties and expressed overlapping positions on several international and domestic issues. Their association continued after Bolsonaro left office, while American criticism of Brazilian judicial proceedings became increasingly prominent during Trump's second presidency.
In October 2026, Reuters reported concerns among foreign diplomats in Brasília about possible American involvement in the political consequences of a closely contested election. Those concerns reflected the unusual diplomatic circumstances surrounding the runoff, but they did not establish that the United States had adopted a policy of rejecting Lula's victory. A reported fear of foreign interference remains different from evidence that the feared action occurred.
Trump's public statements immediately before the result were comparatively restrained. Questioned on October 25 about his position toward the candidates, he said the United States was monitoring the election without declaring support for either candidate in that exchange. Earlier political expressions concerning the Bolsonaro family provide relevant context, but they cannot establish a subsequent decision to impose economic penalties.
The legal significance of Lula's victory lies in the continuity of Brazil's elected government and its existing policy positions. The United States has no supervisory jurisdiction over the TSE, and its political preferences do not determine who holds Brazil's presidency. Washington nevertheless retains considerable influence over bilateral trade and financial relations through instruments governed by American law. Those powers, rather than any authority over Brazil's electoral process, form the basis of the potential economic confrontation.
2. The Lula–Trump Tariffs Already Affecting Brazil
The current trade confrontation cannot be explained through a single tariff percentage. Since 2025, Washington has employed several legal authorities to restrict imports, including emergency economic legislation and provisions of the Trade Act of 1974. Some measures were directed specifically at Brazil; others applied to numerous trading partners. Their rates, exemptions, and legal consequences differ.
The distinction became particularly significant in February 2026, when the Supreme Court rejected the administration's interpretation of its emergency tariff powers. The judgment led to the termination of duties imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), including the Brazil-specific restrictions adopted in July 2025. Separate tariff measures under Sections 232 and 301 remained unaffected.
By the time Lula won reelection, the principal Brazil-specific trade restrictions arose from the July 2026 Section 301 investigation. Their application depends on the products imported, the relevant exemptions, and the relationship between overlapping duties. Assessing the prospect of further escalation requires first establishing the restrictions that were already operating.
2.1 The 2025 Tariffs and the Supreme Court’s Intervention
On July 30, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14323, Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Brazil. The order imposed an additional 40% ad valorem duty on covered Brazilian imports under IEEPA, subject to exemptions and subsequent modifications. Together with previously applicable emergency tariff measures, the order initially produced a headline additional rate of 50% for certain Brazilian products.
The administration justified its action partly through allegations concerning Brazilian judicial proceedings, restrictions on political expression, and the treatment of American technology companies. Those allegations formed part of the executive's stated rationale for declaring an emergency. Their inclusion in a presidential order did not independently establish the legality of imposing customs duties under IEEPA.

articles.title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
articles.summary: VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVsAudi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a b...
articles.full_text:
Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.
The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.
The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.
Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.
Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.
The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.
However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

articles.full_text:
We produce a numerical estimate of the value of unpaid breastfeeding relative to national income spanning five centuries and integrating historical and bioarchaeological data. The relative economic contribution of maternal nursing was greater in the distant past than in recent history, rivaling regionally significant industries such as pottery, glassmaking, and even the historical public sector. It was likely the largest source of human capital investment in early modern England, supporting the physical and cognitive development of the workforce. Finally, we show that breastfeeding rates probably fell as incomes rose, challenging the Malthusian assumption that higher income correlates with lower mortality.
That is from a recent paper by Louis Henderson and Jane Humphries.  Via the excellent Samir Varma.

Dev Goyal received a grant for SCRIPT, exploring whether stylus-based drawing kinematics can support non-diagnostic clinical triage for ADHD, autism, and anxiety.
Adwait Tiwari, 16, a self-taught founder from Indore, is building BharatBahi, a WhatsApp-native AI assistant helping Indian shopkeepers.
Mayukh Goswami and Meher Manda received their grant for a graphic novel examining democratic crises around the world through the lens of a fictional Indian town.
Ajith Chekka is building Oru’el, a physics-enabled intelligence layer to improve the reliability and efficiency of data centers.
Gaurav Kumar, a software engineer and social entrepreneur, is building OncoVault, which turns fragmented cancer records into AI-generated clinical summaries to support physicians’ treatment decisions.
Kush Agrawal, an engineering student at IIT Bombay, received a grant for Tensor Recon, developing execution-aware financial reconciliation infrastructure for high-volume cryptocurrency trading firms.
Mohd. Ashzad, 22, a security researcher and engineer, is building Build Jam, helping young South Asian builders discover creative skills through real-world projects in AI, design, filmmaking, and photography.
Vaibhav Sai, 25, received a grant to develop AI for intent-based biomolecular design, starting with a nucleotide-focused model and capture molecules for biosensors.
Rithvik Vibhu and Rithwik Jayasimha received their grant for research on passive optical fiber network vulnerabilities, including wiretapping and attacks on ISP infrastructure, and presentations at Black Hat USA 2026 and DEF CON 34.
Neha Sarda is building Zyogen, sovereign AI software converting injury images into patient-specific printable graft designs and bioink formulations, aiming to make regenerative medicine 30–40% more affordable.
Hari Shankar Ramalingam, cofounder and CEO of SpaceTug, received a grant to develop and validate autonomous spacecraft technologies for in-orbit satellite servicing, inspection, and life extension, ahead of orbital demonstrations.
Laiba Noor received a travel grant to attend a research program at Özyeğin University and develop a speech-analysis tool for detecting presymptomatic Alzheimer’s in low-resource settings.
Abhishek Raj, 16, a crime and mystery writer and dual national record holder, received a grant to advance his fiction writing and criminology research.
Kunal Kanase, an IIT Bombay pre-doctoral fellow, received a grant for GullyWell, studying Dharavi  residents’ wellbeing where formal mental-health care rarely reaches and developing low-cost tools informed by that research.
Divyaratna Joshi, a Chemical Engineering undergraduate at IIT Madras, is developing low-cost S-PEEK membranes to replace expensive fluorinated membranes and make fuel cells and electrolyzers affordable and manufacturable at scale.
Tanjot Singh, 16, received a grant for PraaNavya (Erynth), a climate startup developing bio-based nanofiber air filtration technology for sustainable clean air.
Tribhi Kathuria, a Lecturer in Robotics at the University of Michigan, received a grant to connect aspiring Indian engineers with robotics and AI research and mentorship from experts in the United States.
Swamynathan Jerra, founder of Hyderabad’s AcquaHT Labs, received a grant to upgrade and seek patents for machines extracting drinking water from air at 30% humidity, rather than the usual 50%, for dry areas with unsafe groundwater.
Niharika Srivastava, a criminal justice and technology lawyer, received a grant to develop a rule-based system identifying Indian undertrial prisoners held beyond statutory custody limits, enabling targeted legal intervention.
Anirudh Varma, a New Delhi pianist, composer, and producer, leads the Anirudh Varma Collective (AVC), received a travel grant for reimagining Indian classical music in a contemporary format for its debut UK tour.
Himaneesh received a grant to build AI software that simplifies professional digital audio workstation workflows.
Sahasrabda Sai Pradhan received a grant to develop a skin-regenerative biomaterial that can be fabricated on-site for urgent graft substitution when suitable tissue is unavailable from the patient’s donor site.
Gaurav Hadavale, 21, a final-year undergraduate at the Sardar Patel Institute of Technology, received a travel grant to present his mechanistic interpretability and trustworthy medical AI research at the MI4MedFM workshop at MICCAI 2026.
M R Sharan, an economist, received a grant to establish a data and intelligence platform focused on India’s local bodies.
Nitish Goel, 14, from Panchkula, is building Thalamus to reduce AI costs and improve efficiency, and Agentoverflow, a shared repository of agents’ solutions that reduces duplicated work and supplies model-training data.
Sudharsanam received a grant for Hardlight, developing autonomous space robots to assemble and maintain assets in low Earth orbit, including space stations, data centers, and factories.
Naveen Gulati, Noida, received a grant for instrumented rooftop trials of GIVARA ONE, a compact dual-rotor vertical-axis turbine for low, gusty winds. Givara Energy owns, installs, and maintains the machines; customers pay only for delivered electricity.

articles.full_text:
How leaders allocate their limited time and attention is an important question in economics. This paper constructs and analyzes a novel data set covering the daily calendars of three Federal Reserve Chairs, Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Jerome Powell, containing more than 20,000 calendar entries. We document several patterns. First, all Fed Chairs spend more than 30% of their documented meetings with Fed staff, highlighting the crucial role of economists in the Fed’s decision process. Second, interactions with the media became more frequent during Bernanke’s tenure and remained important until the end of Powell’s tenure. Third, Powell held significantly more meetings with lawmakers than both Yellen and Bernanke, reflecting an increasing need for the Fed to engage with political actors. Beyond these trend patterns, we examine the time allocation of Fed Chairs at business cycle frequencies and show how different activities respond to shifts in the macroeconomic environment. Finally, we place our findings in historical context using the available calendars of earlier Fed Chairs, including Alan Greenspan.
That is from a recent NBER working paper by  Thomas Drechsel   & Dali Tsakadze.
